title: Colts Open to Trading RB Jonathan Taylor, ESPN Reports Active Negotiations with Multiple Teams
body:
Indianapolis has officially signaled that it is willing to move its premier running back, Jonathan Taylor, as the franchise evaluates its roster and salary‑cap outlook for the 2027 season. Sources close to the organization told both ESPN and NFL Network that the Colts front office has opened trade discussions, and several clubs have already expressed interest in acquiring the former MVP candidate. While no formal offer has been lodged, the willingness to entertain a deal marks a dramatic shift for a team that has long viewed Taylor as the cornerstone of its offense.

Taylor, who entered the league as a first‑round pick in 2020 and quickly established himself as one of the NFL’s most productive rushers, posted a modest 2026 campaign that still ranked among the league’s top ten in rushing yards. However, his contract—valued at $12 million for the upcoming season—has become a focal point in the Colts’ cap calculations. The team is projected to be $4 million over the salary floor after accounting for free‑agent commitments and the looming extensions of key defensive players. Trading Taylor could free up significant cap space, allowing Indianapolis to retain its defensive core while pursuing upgrades at quarterback and edge‑rusher positions.

The trade market for Taylor appears surprisingly robust. Early reports indicate that the Miami Dolphins, Dallas Cowboys, and New York Giants have opened preliminary talks, each seeing the running back as a potential answer to their own offensive deficiencies. Miami, still reeling from an injury‑plagued backfield, views Taylor as a complementary piece to rookie sensation Raheem Mostert. Dallas, which has struggled to establish a consistent ground game behind Ezekiel Elliott’s decline, hopes a veteran like Taylor could provide a balanced attack alongside a rejuvenated passing offense. The Giants, meanwhile, are looking to add a proven workhorse to support Daniel Jones, whose mobility has become a critical component of New York’s play‑calling.

Analysts caution that the value the Colts can extract may be tempered by Taylor’s recent injury history. A lingering ankle issue forced him to miss three games last season, and medical evaluations will likely play a pivotal role in any final agreement. Moreover, the NFL’s evolving offensive philosophies—favoring passing over rushing—have depressed the market for top‑tier running backs in recent years. Teams are generally hesitant to surrender high draft capital for a position that, while still valuable, does not command the same premium as elite quarterbacks or pass rushers. Consequently, the Colts could be looking at a mid‑round draft pick package, possibly supplemented by a later‑round selection, rather than the high‑value return they might have hoped for a few years ago.

From a strategic standpoint, the potential departure of Taylor could catalyze a broader shift in Indianapolis’ offensive identity. Head coach Shane Stewart has already hinted at a more “dynamic” scheme that leans on play‑action and spread concepts, reducing reliance on a single bell‑cow. By reallocating the cap space freed up by a trade, the Colts could target a versatile quarterback—perhaps a veteran like Derek Carr or a rising star such as Bryce Young—while also bolstering the defensive line with a Pro Bowl‑caliber edge rusher. The trade would also open opportunities for younger backs on the roster, like rookie Jalen Miller, to assume larger roles and develop under reduced pressure.

The coming weeks will be critical as the trade deadline approaches. If Indianapolis secures a satisfactory return, the move could reshape the AFC South power balance, giving the Colts a fresh financial footing and a chance to retool before free agency. Conversely, if negotiations stall, Taylor will likely report to training camp, and the Colts will have to decide whether to retain him at a premium cost or risk a potential locker‑room distraction. Either scenario underscores a pivotal moment for a franchise that has long depended on a single running back to anchor its offense, and the outcome will reverberate through the league’s offseason strategies.
